title: William Howard Taft
description: President of the United States from 1909 to 1913
wiki_lead:
William Howard Taft (September 15, 1857 – March 8, 1930) was the 27th president of the United States from 1909 to 1913 and the tenth chief justice of the United States from 1921 to 1930. He is the only person to have held both offices.
Taft was born in Cincinnati, Ohio. His father, Alphonso Taft, was a U.S. attorney general and secretary of war. Taft attended Yale University and the Cincinnati Law School. After becoming a lawyer, he was appointed a judge while still in his twenties and continued a rapid rise, being named solicitor general and a judge of the Sixth Circuit Court of Appeals in the 1890s. President William McKinley appointed Taft civilian governor of the Philippines in 1901. President Theodore Roosevelt made him secretary of war in 1904, and he became Roosevelt's hand-picked successor. With Roosevelt's help, Taft easily won the Republican nomination for president in 1908 and defeated William Jennings Bryan for the presidency in the  general election.
As president, Taft focused on East Asia more than European affairs and repeatedly intervened to prop up or remove Latin American governments. While Taft sought reductions to trade tariffs, the resulting bill was heavily influenced by special interests. His administration was filled with conflict between the Republican Party's conservative wing, with which Taft often sympathized, and its progressive wing, towards which Roosevelt increasingly gravitated. Controversies over conservation and antitrust cases filed by the Taft administration served to further separate the two men. The 1912 presidential election was a three-way race, as Roosevelt challenged Taft for renomination. Taft used his control of the party machinery to gain a bare majority of delegates and Roosevelt bolted the party. The split left Taft with little chance of reelection, and he took only Utah and Vermont in his loss to Democratic nominee Woodrow Wilson.
After leaving office, Taft returned to Yale as a professor, continuing his political activity and working against war through the League to Enforce Peace. Despite his personal ambition to become chief justice, Taft had previously declined repeated offers of appointment to the Supreme Court of the United States, believing his political work to be more important. In 1921, President Warren G. Harding appointed Taft chief justice. As a member of the court, he was a conservative on business issues, and under him there were advances in individual rights. His work towards administrative reform of the court culminated in the Judiciary Act of 1925. In poor health, he resigned in February 1930, and died the following month. He was buried at Arlington National Cemetery, the first president and first Supreme Court justice to be interred there.
Taft is generally listed near the middle in historians' rankings of U.S. presidents; his work as chief justice has been evaluated more positively. In popular memory his political achievements and role in Republican Party history have been overshadowed by his weight and physical appearance.

grok_lead: William Howard Taft (September 15, 1857 â March 8, 1930) was an American jurist and statesman who served as the 27th president of the United States from 1909 to 1913 and the tenth chief justice of the United States from 1921 to 1930, the only person to hold both offices. A Republican from Ohio, Taft graduated from Yale College in 1878, pursued a legal career, and held various judicial and administrative roles before entering national politics, including serving as U.S. solicitor general from 1890 to 1892, a federal judge from 1892 to 1900, the first civilian governor-general of the Philippines from 1900 to 1903, and U.S. Secretary of War from 1904 to 1908. Hand-picked by President Theodore Roosevelt as his successor, Taft won the 1908 election decisively, securing 321 electoral votes against Democrat William Jennings Bryan's 162. His administration continued progressive-era reforms, prosecuting over 75 antitrust casesâmore than under Rooseveltâestablishing a postal savings system, and expanding federal conservation efforts, though the Payne-Aldrich Tariff Act of 1909, intended to lower duties but resulting in modest reductions, alienated many in his party and fueled the rise of the Progressive faction. Taft's presidency ended in defeat amid a party split with Roosevelt in 1912, allowing Democrat Woodrow Wilson to win; Taft received just 8 electoral votes, the fewest of any incumbent seeking reelection. Appointed chief justice by President Warren G. Harding in 1921, Taft prioritized judicial efficiency, authoring 253 opinions during his tenure and advocating for a new Supreme Court building, fulfilling his lifelong preference for the bench over elective office.
